aicontainers.headline: AI Research Container Platform
aicontainers.intro: Designed and built an entire container framework at JP Morgan for running cutting edge research containers, giving several research teams a fast, reliable way to run their AI research.
explanation: Alongside my work on JP Morgan's internal Jupyter platform, I designed and built an entire container framework for running cutting edge research containers. AI research moves incredibly quickly and researchers need to be able to try new models, libraries and toolchains as soon as they are released. The aim of the framework was to make that possible inside the bank, without every research team having to become infrastructure experts.

AI workloads come with a very particular set of challenges. Research images are large and tied to specific CUDA and driver versions, experiments need access to scarce and expensive GPU resources, and everything has to run safely within the controls of a highly regulated organisation. On top of this, every research team has its own preferred tools, so the framework needed to be flexible enough to support all of them whilst still being a consistent and supportable platform.

The framework is built on standard container technology. Research environments are packaged as Docker / OCI images and run on Kubernetes, which schedules the workloads onto NVIDIA GPUs. The framework's tooling is written in Python, giving researchers a simple way to define, launch and manage their research containers.
The platform is now used by several research teams across JP Morgan to run their AI research, letting them spend their time on the research itself rather than on the infrastructure underneath it.
outcomes: Designed and built an entire container framework for running cutting edge AI research containers
Adopted by several research teams across JP Morgan to run their AI research
GPU accelerated research workloads packaged as containers and scheduled on Kubernetes
Researchers can pick up the latest models and tooling quickly without managing infrastructure themselves

ukhsa.headline: Fighting COVID with UKHSA
ukhsa.intro: As part of the UK Health Security Agency's response to the coronavirus pandemic, I worked in a data specialist role spanning analysis, data science, data engineering and DevOps, and won an award for my contributions to the civil service.
explanation: In November 2020, I joined the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), then known as the Joint Biosecurity Centre, as a contractor, with the goal of using data and data science to fight the coronavirus pandemic. I was assigned to a new team using wastewater (sewage) data to detect outbreaks and measure cases in an area. This was a cutting edge implementation of wastewater based epidemiology at a scale never before seen anywhere in the world.

My first project was producing bespoke visualisations for this new data source. We were measuring the amount of COVID molecules in wastewater samples, which is not an easily understood metric, so it was vital that our figures were concise and digestible. We produced reports with these figures for decision makers such as public health officials, who used them to shape public health policy. At this stage the process was still very manual and, with a constant stream of new data arriving each day, it took up most of the team's week, so I began automating it.

My first automation ran our figure producing code and generated slide decks in a fixed format with the latest figures added. This freed up the majority of the team's time, as I could now do the job that previously took three of us all week, and let the team focus on other improvements. I then went further and, on my own initiative, rewrote all of the automation and figure producing code to create a fully interactive report that worked like a dashboard. This allowed far deeper investigation of our data and could show more of it without static figures becoming cluttered. This work was hugely significant and I won an award for my contributions to the civil service.

Another large area of my work was data engineering, where I did much of the design and build of our solution. We wanted as much data about the pandemic as possible to produce the best insights, so I was regularly building new and more sophisticated datasets. This took cleaning and processing away from our data scientists, giving them simple access to reliable, ready to use datasets and saving the organisation many hours that could be spent on other problems.

Our data engineering solution was fully cloud based, and I was instrumental in deploying the entire solution as infrastructure as code. Using the AWS Cloud Development Kit, the whole solution could be rapidly redeployed and fully functional simply by deploying our code.
I also ran educational sessions on Git and general cloud practices for the wider team, many of whom had no prior experience with these technologies.
outcomes: Won an award for my contributions to the civil service
Automated reporting that previously took three people all week, generating tens of thousands of pounds in efficiency savings
Early and accurate outbreak detection that improved health outcomes
Created a machine learning and rules based system, using a proprietary algorithm, to identify high risk areas and assign risk scores
Moved the data engineering solution to infrastructure as code, allowing rapid deployment and scale ups
Built end-to-end data pipelines providing high quality, validated datasets for scientific analysis
Developed interactive visualisations that made insights easier to find and improved information for policy makers

insuranceai.headline: AI Health Insurance Pricing
insuranceai.intro: Built a reasoning engine and natural language processing pipeline that automatically priced health and life insurance applications from customers' medical histories, cutting quote times from 6 weeks to minutes and saving over £10M.
explanation: This project was a cutting edge use of natural language processing and cognitive reasoning which, at the time, made Aviva the only insurance company in the UK with this capability. It used the medical history data customers already provided when applying for health and life insurance, passing it through our pipeline to remove the need for a human underwriter.

Before this, it could take as long as 6 weeks for a customer to receive a quote after submitting their request, which was bad for both the customer and the business. Automating the process allowed a much faster throughput of cases, and by handling the majority of them it let underwriters focus their expertise on the few cases that were particularly complex or where the system had low confidence in its predictions. These time and efficiency savings were expected to save the company over £10M in just a few years.

There were large challenges to overcome, not least whether the solution was even possible. As it was world leading, there were no guides or articles to follow and we had to break new ground. Relying heavily on NLP also brought its own problems, particularly as medical records were often verbatim dictated text or even shorthand.

The solution had two main components: an NLP engine (IBM Watson) and an entirely in-house reasoning engine. When a customer applied online, their medical history was downloaded and passed into the NLP engine, which extracted conditions, symptoms and other relevant health information, along with the links between them and its confidence in each link. This was passed into our reasoning engine, which used the extracted statements to build a 'health profile' estimating the likelihood of many diseases and conditions. It also took into account other relevant information such as family history, height, weight, age and medications, and adjusted for time, since something that happened long ago is less relevant to pricing today. From this profile it calculated the expected price for each insurance product.

The system successfully priced over 70% of the cases fed into it, allowing all of the predicted business savings to be achieved and significantly reducing the time customers waited for quotes. As far as I am aware, the system is still live in production.
outcomes: Business savings in excess of £10M from faster, automated pricing
Quote wait times reduced from 6 weeks to minutes
Over 70% of cases priced automatically, freeing underwriters to focus on complex cases
Form based responses also priced automatically, delivering further savings of ~£1M

softwarevalidation.headline: Highly Secure Software Validation
softwarevalidation.intro: Created a platform that validated and inspected all ingested software for malicious behaviour before storing it in an assured database for secure access, delivered on time and within budget.
explanation: Whilst working with BT, I helped deliver a highly secure solution as part of a multi-billion pound project. Due to the sensitive nature of the work I can't discuss much of what was done, but this breakdown covers as much as I can share.

My work centred on the entry point for software coming onto the platform. Security was of the utmost importance, so we built an entry point where users could upload files to be analysed. Once a piece of software had been analysed it either passed or failed, and software that passed could be moved through to the secure area.

The focus on security brought some huge challenges. Our code needed to be secure and tested to highly rigorous standards. The system was also installed on premises and entirely air-gapped, so we couldn't easily run and test our code on the target hardware, which mattered because the software evaluations were computationally heavy.

The solution had several parts. It needed to move potentially very large files through without issue, apply state of the art cyber security capabilities to break down and inspect those files, store both the files and significant metadata and results about them in a database, and provide a bespoke web application through which the files could be viewed and downloaded. As one of the lead developers, I contributed to every one of these areas.

File movement was handled by Apache NiFi, for which we also built custom processors so it integrated cleanly with the other components. NiFi was the backbone of the solution, taking files, passing them to components that wrote them to another location, then picking them up again to move them through the process. For the security analysis we implemented multiple systems, both developed internally and integrated from external products, aiming to cover every aspect of software investigation and give the highest possible confidence in the files. Processed files and their metadata were stored in Elasticsearch, and I used this data to build a frontend that displayed the files and their metadata, with search, filtering and sorting across a wide range of characteristics.

We built the solution on time and within budget, which was critical as other areas of the wider programme depended on us and any delay would have cascaded down the line. We also fully automated the deployment, so the solution could be redeployed in the event of an outage, and did so modularly so that any individual VM or service could be rebuilt quickly. Finally, we repurposed the previous solution into a test environment to make future development far easier.
outcomes: Delivered on time and within budget, preventing costly delays in a £1.5bn project
Fully automated Ansible deployment, building the solution onto VMs with no manual configuration
Profiled and redesigned the system for higher efficiency on new hardware
Packaged the solution as a series of Linux services for easy running and monitoring

mlgui.headline: Machine Learning GUI
mlgui.intro: A graphical user interface for building machine learning models on a complex World Bank economic dataset, with models and results stored in a database for fast recall.
explanation: This was a personal project I started after discovering a fascinating dataset from the World Bank. The World Development Indicators cover over 250 countries, 50 years and thousands of fields, with over 1 million data points about economic development. I was eager to explore it, and after a while I had built many models and gathered plenty of insights.
I realised that an application handling the most common things I wanted to do with the dataset would let me explore it far more efficiently, while storing my results to share in future.

The main challenge was generalising the machine learning code so that any features and parameters could be passed in from selections made in the app. This also created a design challenge: keeping the app simple and easy to use while offering enough options that it didn't feel limiting.

The frontend was built with ReactJS and offered selection components for choosing the parameters, and optionally hyperparameters, to pass into the chosen machine learning model. Submitted queries went to a NodeJS backend, which handled most of the communication between components. The backend first checked a MongoDB database and returned existing results if they were already there. Otherwise it called a second web API written in Python with Flask, which integrated easily with the machine learning scripts I had written using standard data science libraries. The results were passed back to the NodeJS backend, written to the database for quick recall next time, and returned to the frontend with some simple visualisations.

The project achieved everything I set out to do: I could explore the dataset far more effectively while saving my results for later. For a time I also hosted the app in the cloud so that friends and colleagues could explore the dataset too.
outcomes: Bespoke system allowing selection of any features, time ranges and countries across many different machine learning methods
All results and models saved to a NoSQL database for faster recall when the same parameters were entered again
Hosted entirely in the cloud on AWS

socialmediagraph.headline: Social Media Community Connectedness
socialmediagraph.intro: An investigation into Reddit communities, applying several graph algorithms to measure how interconnected they are.
explanation: This project investigated a large social media dataset describing interactions from one community to another. For each interaction the dataset included the source and target community, when it occurred, and some sentiment analysis and other properties.
I thought this was a very rich dataset and wanted to implement some graph theory algorithms myself to measure properties of the communities, particularly how they are interconnected.

The biggest challenge was that graph algorithms on large graphs need a lot of computing power, especially as the ones I implemented don't scale linearly with graph size. To mitigate this I often worked on smaller subsets of the data, then applied the algorithms to larger datasets once I knew they worked, though I was still heavily constrained by computing resources.

The main algorithms I implemented were Karger's and Girvan-Newman's, as I knew both and expected them to give interesting results. Karger's algorithm computes a minimum cut of a connected graph: the fewest edges that need to be removed to split the graph into two disjoint components. It works by repeatedly picking an edge at random and merging the two nodes it connects (removing self loops) until only two nodes remain, at which point the number of remaining edges gives a candidate minimum cut. Girvan-Newman's algorithm, which I used to measure how connected communities are, detects community structure using edge betweenness centrality (how many shortest paths between nodes pass through an edge). It calculates the betweenness centrality of every edge, removes the edge with the highest value, recalculates, and repeats until no edges remain. As it runs, the network splits into communities, and the results can be shown as a dendrogram.

I implemented these algorithms in both Python and Apache Spark. The Girvan-Newman results were particularly interesting and matched what I intuitively expected, for example showing high connectedness between political communities, or between sports communities, but much lower connectedness between a sports community and a political one. This was reassuring, since people who like sports are likely to engage across many sports communities, and likewise for politics, without necessarily crossing between the two.
outcomes: Implemented graph algorithms including Karger's and Girvan-Newman's in both Python and Apache Spark
Results matched expected community behaviour, giving high confidence in the implementations
Enabled deeper investigation of how social media communities interact, with visualisations of large community graphs

cybersecurity.headline: Cyber Security Data Science Hub
cybersecurity.intro: A collection of projects building, exploring and applying data science in a cyber security context across a wide range of use cases.
explanation: Whilst at BT I worked in the cyber security Data Science Hub (DSH), a team set up to apply data science to new areas of cyber security. This ranged from improving existing projects and products, to building new solutions, to exploring whether novel ideas were viable. I worked across several projects during my time in the team, a few of which are summarised here.

One project was an evaluation of Apache Metron, a highly scalable, open source security analytics framework. BT Security wanted to know whether it could become the next big thing in cyber security frameworks, so I led a piece of work evaluating it.

As an early stage product it came with the problems you would expect, such as bugs, crashes and installation issues. Once most of these were resolved I was able to evaluate its capabilities and how easily it could be used and extended.

My findings were shared across BT Security, particularly with the team working on a similar product we offered, allowing them to incorporate some of Metron's best features and designs into our offering. I also presented some of these findings to external customers as an example of the cutting edge investigations BT Security was undertaking.
Another project involved terabytes of netflow traffic data, investigating whether it was feasible to extract useful insights or whether the data was simply too large and noisy.

I was involved early on, helping to design the investigation and build the early implementation. Using a collection of AWS products we first generated large volumes of synthetic data to check whether the solution could process it fast enough, then gradually made the generated data an accurate imitation of real netflow data. We found the system could handle the processing, showing that gathering insights was feasible.

I also completed several courses while in the DSH. The most significant was a week long practical ethical hacking course from EC-Council, covering areas such as footprinting, vulnerability analysis and system hacking. Another was a multi-day intensive course on Apache Spark, the big data framework widely used in security where datasets are often very large, covering everything from the basics to advanced algorithm implementations.
outcomes: Evaluation of a cutting edge security analytics platform led to its features being incorporated into BT Security products
Early work on terabytes of netflow data produced a prototype and proved that gathering insights was feasible
Completed cyber security and big data courses including ethical hacking (EC-Council) and Apache Spark

llmcodegen.headline: AI-Assisted Development
llmcodegen.intro: I have used AI tools since their inception and always work at the cutting edge, from generating a complete web app with early LLMs to building and shipping software with today's AI coding agents.
explanation: I have been using AI tools for software development since they first appeared, and I make a point of always working with the latest models and tooling. This project follows how that workflow has evolved, from early experiments to the way I build software today.

My first experiment, in 2023, was building a complete colour palette web app using only code generated by OpenAI's GPT-3.5. Working through a chat interface, I iterated on prompts to generate colour manipulation, palette selection, dynamic rendering, transitions and user interface components. It showed that AI could genuinely accelerate development, and taught me a lot about prompting effectively and about keeping generated TypeScript type safe.

Today my workflow is built around AI coding agents that work directly in the codebase, including Claude Code, GitHub Copilot and bespoke internal AI tooling at JP Morgan. Rather than copying snippets from a chat window, I give agents well scoped tasks, the context they need and clear ways to verify their work, then review, test and refine what they produce. This lets me move much faster across the whole development lifecycle, from exploring unfamiliar code and prototyping ideas to refactoring, writing tests and shipping changes.

Keeping up with a field that moves this quickly is part of the job. I continually try new models and tools as they are released and bring the ones that prove themselves into my everyday work, while keeping the code review and testing discipline that makes AI generated code safe to ship.
outcomes: Using AI tools for development since their inception, consistently adopting the latest models and agents
Claude Code, GitHub Copilot and bespoke internal AI tooling embedded in my everyday workflow, from prototyping to production changes
Built a complete web app using only LLM generated code as an early experiment
Link to app: https://colourpicker-073t.onrender.com/

jpm.headline: JP Morgan Quant Enablement
jpm.intro: Improving productivity for thousands of quantitative researchers by building and maintaining JP Morgan's internal Jupyter platform, one of the firm's most successful internal technology products.
explanation: At JP Morgan, I am part of a team building an extensive internal platform for quant enablement, focused on our internal Jupyter offering. It gives our quantitative researchers seamless access to the Jupyter ecosystem and related technologies such as Voilà and nbconvert.

Our team maintains and continuously improves the internal Jupyter service, which serves thousands of users across the organisation and consistently receives high satisfaction from them. Our enhancements include numerous internal extensions that integrate with other JP Morgan frameworks, giving researchers a smooth and efficient workflow for their research and analysis.
We also contribute to the wider open source Jupyter community, including Jupyter Filesystems, which benefits the broader ecosystem as well as JP Morgan.

We recently rebuilt our Jupyter offering to support both on premises and cloud environments. This hybrid approach gives users greater flexibility and scalability, accommodates diverse computational needs and ensures high availability.
outcomes: Serving thousands of quantitative researchers across the firm, with consistently high user satisfaction
Rebuilt the Jupyter offering to run both on premises and in the cloud for greater flexibility and scalability
Built internal extensions integrating Jupyter with other JP Morgan frameworks
Contributed to the open source Jupyter ecosystem, including Jupyter Filesystems

magicbreakfast.headline: Magic Breakfast Schools Portal
magicbreakfast.intro: Led a team of six developers to deliver a schools portal for the charity Magic Breakfast, on time and under budget, winning JP Morgan's award for the most sustainable project.
explanation: As part of the JP Morgan Force for Good programme, which pairs JPM technologists with charities looking to improve their technology, I led a project for the charity Magic Breakfast. Our goal was a schools portal that would streamline operations for Magic Breakfast and their partner schools.

The portal is a central hub where schools can access order information and important resources. Because schools can now find this information themselves, they no longer need to contact the charity directly, saving time and reducing administrative overhead. The web application includes the features expected of a modern web app, such as account management, and is built and hosted on WordPress.

As technical lead, I guided a team of six developers to deliver the project on time and under budget, and our work was recognised internally at JP Morgan with the award for the most sustainable project. Magic Breakfast described the portal as transformational for their operations, and chose to take part in the Force for Good programme again the following year.
The project showed how technology can drive social good, and I look forward to more opportunities to create meaningful change through technology.
outcomes: Recognised with JP Morgan's award for the most sustainable project
Estimated staff time savings of hundreds of hours over the portal's lifetime
Delivered on schedule and within Magic Breakfast's budget, leading a team of six developers
Researched the problem space and potential solutions, sharing our analysis with the Magic Breakfast team
